newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai Huili hurt by poison rumours.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Huili hurt by poison rumours.

text.p: China's paint producer Shanghai Huili Building Materials Co Ltd is suffering plummeting sales of its main paint and coating products due to rumours that they contain poison, an official said on Wednesday.

The rumours stem from an incident in the southwest province of Sichuan last year in which a man died in his sleep in his freshly painted room. The word spread that the wall coating was made by Huili and sales began to fall.

"We sent people out to check on the case and it appears the man had been drinking and may have become too excited with his girlfriend," said company accountant Wang Ruili in an interview. "It had nothing to do with the coating on the walls."
"We have done tests and there is no poison in the coatings at all, it is just rumours," she added.
But the poison rumours were already out there and Huili, which listed B shares on the Shanghai stock exchange in June, saw sales of its coatings start to fall from the second half of last year.
Coatings accounted for 50 percent of the company's profits before the rumours but have now dropped to 40 percent and are still falling.
Overall profits are falling too as a result. The company reported a net profit of 80 million yuan ($9.64 million) in 1994, but only 48 million in 1995.
In the first half of 1996, its post-tax profit was 10.3 million yuan, it said in its interim report but gave no year-earlier comparison.
On Wednesday, the stock was trading around $0.186, down from a year-high of $0.234.
"The first half of this year was bad. The second half will be better, but we will still see a further fall in profits. The main reason is the rumours," Wang said.
A secondary factor affecting sales, she said, was widespread piracy of Huili products, particularly by factories in the southern Guangdong province.
Huili has gone after companies passing off their products as its goods but has received little support from the local authorities, she said.
"This is regional protectionism. In one case the authorities simply fined the company 100 yuan and that's it," she said.
To offset the rumour problem, the company is trying to boost sales of other products, particularly floorboards and doors for use in newly built homes.
Wang declined to make any prediction on profits for 1997, but said the overall outlook for the construction industry was good.

Fixed-asset investment was a major target of an austerity programme launched by the government in July 1993. But falling inflation and two cuts in interest rates this year have spurred growth in the construction sector.
Based in Shanghai, Huili has a staff of 1,500, net assets of 200 million yuan and its goods include coatings, waterproof materials, metal ceilings, curtains and doors.
